questions.question: Diwali is often called the festival of what?
questions.explanation: Families light small clay lamps called diyas, and there are often fireworks too.

questions.question: On Bonfire Night, people remember a plot to blow up which building?
questions.explanation: Guy Fawkes was caught on 5 November with barrels of gunpowder hidden under Parliament.

questions.question: For how many nights is Hanukkah celebrated?
questions.explanation: One more candle is lit on the menorah each night, until all eight are burning.

questions.question: In the Chinese zodiac, each year is named after one of how many animals?
questions.explanation: The twelve animals take turns, starting with the Rat and ending with the Pig.

questions.question: Which royal helped make Christmas trees popular in Britain in the 1840s?
questions.explanation: Queen Victoria's German husband loved Christmas trees, and a picture of the royal family round one in 1848 started a craze.

questions.question: Before pumpkins, which vegetable did people in Ireland and Scotland carve into Halloween lanterns?
questions.explanation: Turnips are much harder to carve than pumpkins, which took over once the tradition reached America.

questions.question: What is the festival that marks the end of Ramadan called?
questions.explanation: Eid al-Fitr traditionally begins when the new crescent moon is seen, with prayers, new clothes, presents and big family meals.

questions.question: During Ramadan, many Muslims do not eat or drink during which part of the day?
questions.explanation: The fast is broken each evening at sunset with a meal called iftar, often starting with dates.

questions.question: Which day, just before Lent begins, is famous for pancakes?
questions.explanation: Pancakes used up the eggs, milk and butter before Lent, and some towns still hold pancake races.

questions.question: Which Australian animal is sometimes used there instead of the Easter Bunny?
questions.explanation: The bilby is a threatened animal with big rabbit-like ears, and chocolate Easter bilbies help raise money to protect it.

questions.question: Which country has given London the giant Christmas tree in Trafalgar Square every year since 1947?
questions.explanation: The tree is a thank-you from the people of Oslo for Britain's help during the Second World War.

questions.question: On which date do many Orthodox Christians, such as in Russia and Serbia, celebrate Christmas Day?
questions.explanation: These churches follow the old Julian calendar, which is now 13 days behind the one most of us use.

questions.question: What colour are the envelopes of money given as presents at Chinese New Year?
questions.explanation: Red is a lucky colour in Chinese culture, so the envelopes, lanterns and decorations are red too.

questions.question: The Day of the Dead, with colourful sugar skulls and marigolds, is a famous festival in which country?
questions.explanation: Families build bright altars to remember loved ones who have died, and it is a happy celebration rather than a sad one.

questions.question: Thanksgiving in the USA always falls on which day of the week?
questions.explanation: It is held on the fourth Thursday of November, usually with a big roast turkey.

questions.question: In which year did the Gunpowder Plot take place?
questions.explanation: The plotters planned to kill King James I at the State Opening of Parliament on 5 November 1605.

questions.question: For Sikhs, Diwali coincides with Bandi Chhor Divas, which marks the release from prison of which Guru?
questions.explanation: Guru Hargobind returned to Amritsar, where the Golden Temple was lit up to welcome him.

questions.question: Hanukkah marks the rededication of the Temple in which city?
questions.explanation: Tradition says one day's oil kept the Temple lamp burning for eight days, which is why Hanukkah lasts eight nights.

questions.question: Which Hindu festival is known for throwing brightly coloured powder to welcome spring?
questions.explanation: Holi is celebrated at a full moon, usually in March, and the night before, bonfires are lit for Holika Dahan.

questions.question: What is the name for the 40 days before Easter in the Christian calendar?
questions.explanation: Lent begins on Ash Wednesday and recalls the Bible story of the 40 days Jesus spent in the desert.

questions.question: Eid al-Adha falls during the annual pilgrimage to which city?
questions.explanation: Eid al-Adha falls during the Hajj, the pilgrimage every Muslim who is able is asked to make at least once.

questions.question: In which country did the Christmas cracker begin?
questions.explanation: The London sweet maker Tom Smith invented it in the 1840s, and the bang was added later.

questions.question: What is New Year's Eve called in Scotland?
questions.explanation: In first-footing, the first visitor after midnight brings gifts such as coal, shortbread or whisky for luck.

questions.question: Which Christmas carol was first performed in Oberndorf, Austria, on Christmas Eve 1818?
questions.explanation: Joseph Mohr wrote the words and Franz Xaver Gruber the tune, and it was first sung with a guitar.

questions.question: Which Jewish festival marks the start of the new year?
questions.explanation: A ram's horn called a shofar is blown, and apples dipped in honey wish everyone a sweet year.

questions.question: Chinese New Year in 2025 began the Year of which animal?
questions.explanation: The Snake followed the Year of the Dragon in 2024, and was followed by the Horse in 2026.

questions.question: Whose saint's day is celebrated in Wales on 1 March?
questions.explanation: St David is the patron saint of Wales, and people wear daffodils or leeks on his day.

questions.question: According to Dutch tradition, Sinterklaas arrives each November by steamboat from which country?
questions.explanation: Sinterklaas brings presents on the evening of 5 December, the eve of St Nicholas's Day.

questions.question: In Italian folklore, which kindly witch brings presents to children on the eve of Epiphany?
questions.explanation: On the night of 5 January she flies on her broomstick, leaving sweets for good children and coal for naughty ones.

questions.question: Which festival, created in 1966, is celebrated in the USA from 26 December to 1 January?
questions.explanation: Kwanzaa celebrates African American culture, with a candle lit on each of its seven days.

questions.question: Whose saint's day, on 17 March, is Ireland's national day?
questions.explanation: The city of Chicago even dyes its river bright green for the celebrations.

questions.question: On which day do people traditionally dance around a maypole?
questions.explanation: Each dancer holds a long ribbon, and as they weave in and out the ribbons are plaited around the pole.

questions.question: What do people in the USA celebrate on 4 July?
questions.explanation: It marks the day in 1776 when the Declaration of Independence was adopted, breaking away from Britain.

questions.question: In Japan, which takeaway food has become a hugely popular Christmas treat?
questions.explanation: A 1970s advert called 'Kentucky for Christmas' started it, and some families order their bucket weeks ahead.

questions.question: In Spain, people eat twelve of which fruit at midnight on New Year's Eve, one for each chime of the clock?
questions.explanation: They are called the twelve grapes of luck, and getting them all down in time is harder than it sounds.

questions.question: In the UK, by what time of day are April Fools' tricks traditionally supposed to stop?
questions.explanation: Anyone who plays a trick after that is said to be the fool themselves.

questions.question: What is the spinning top that children play with at Hanukkah called?
questions.explanation: Each of its four sides has a Hebrew letter, and the side it lands on decides whether you win sweets or chocolate coins.

questions.question: At which Chinese festival do families share round mooncakes and admire the full moon?
questions.explanation: It falls on the 15th day of the eighth month of the Chinese calendar, when the moon is said to be at its brightest.

questions.question: Boxing Day, 26 December, is also the feast day of which saint?
questions.explanation: That is why the carol says Good King Wenceslas looked out 'on the Feast of Stephen'.

questions.question: Halloween falls on the night before which special day?
questions.explanation: Halloween is short for All Hallows' Eve, and 'hallow' is an old word for a saint.

questions.question: Which Christmas plant with white berries are people supposed to kiss under?
questions.explanation: The custom goes back at least to the 1700s in England.

questions.question: Which spiced bun with a cross on top is traditionally eaten at Easter?
questions.explanation: They are traditionally eaten on Good Friday, the day Christians remember Jesus dying on the cross.

questions.question: Counting Rudolph, how many reindeer pull Santa's sleigh?
questions.explanation: Dasher, Dancer, Prancer, Vixen, Comet, Cupid, Donner and Blitzen, with Rudolph leading the way.

questions.question: In the Netherlands, what do children leave by the fireplace for Sinterklaas to fill with sweets?
questions.explanation: Some children put a carrot or hay in the shoe for Sinterklaas's horse.

questions.question: At Diwali, what are the little clay oil lamps that people light called?
questions.explanation: Rows of diyas light the way for Lakshmi, the goddess of good fortune.

questions.question: Which saint, said to have slain a dragon, is England's patron saint, remembered on 23 April?
questions.explanation: His red cross on a white background is the flag of England.

questions.question: What is the name for the four weeks leading up to Christmas?
questions.explanation: The word comes from the Latin for 'coming', and it is why we open Advent calendars.

questions.question: In 'The Twelve Days of Christmas', what does my true love give me on the fifth day?
questions.explanation: Singers traditionally slow right down and belt out 'five go-old rings'.

questions.question: Which Jewish festival remembers the Israelites' escape from slavery in Egypt?
questions.explanation: Families share a special meal, the Seder, with flat bread called matzah.

questions.question: In which decade was the first commercial Christmas card sent in Britain?
questions.explanation: Henry Cole (later Sir Henry) had about 1,000 printed in 1843, to save himself writing lots of Christmas letters.
